summary: Describes the Message Tracking Query Protocol, which is used with an SMTP tracking extension to find the path a message took and its current routing status within a messaging system.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the way to ask a mail system, "Where did my message go, and where is it now?"

questions: how to find the status of an email message
what is the message tracking query protocol
how does the mtqp track command work
how do i track an email message through smtp servers
subtitle: A line-oriented protocol for asking a mail system where a message went and what happened to it.

tldr.problem: Customers of enterprise message systems ask whether they can track a message: find the path it took and its current routing status.
tldr.mechanism: MTQP is a text protocol on TCP port 1038. A client sends a TRACK command with a message's tracking id and secret, and the server answers with message/tracking-status data.
tldr.outcome: Together with an SMTP extension and the tracking-status MIME type, it forms a complete message tracking solution. The RFC was later updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3887 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996, so check those for changes.

sections.title: What MTQP Is For
sections.content:
Message tracking is the ability to find out the path a message has taken through a messaging system and its current routing status. The Message Tracking Query Protocol (MTQP) is one of three companion pieces. One memo defines an SMTP extension that provides the information needed to track messages, another defines the message/tracking-status media type used to report status, and this memo defines the protocol for querying the status of messages sent over SMTP.

In the terminology of the model document, the solution uses active enabling and active requests, with both request and chaining referrals.
sections.plainLanguage: People want to know where their email has been. This is the part of the system that answers that question when you ask.

sections.title: Connections, Commands and Responses
sections.content:
MTQP is line-oriented, like POP3 and NNTP. A server listens on TCP port 1038. The client finds the server host with a DNS SRV lookup using service name mtqp and protocol tcp, such as _mtqp._tcp.smtp3.example.com. If no SRV records exist, it falls back to an address record lookup. A mail system that wants tracking queries handled on a different machine from its mail server MUST publish an SRV MTQP record pointing there, and the tracking service MUST be able to answer queries for all messages that mail system accepted.

Commands are a case-insensitive keyword plus optional parameters, ended by CRLF, in printable ASCII, and limited to 998 characters before the CRLF. Responses start with a status indicator: +OK for success, +OK+ for success followed by more lines, -TEMP for a temporary failure, -ERR for a permanent failure and -BAD for a protocol error. Indicators can be followed by slash-separated machine-readable response information, then optional human-readable text meant for logs, not end users.

A multi-line response ends with a line holding a single period. Any data line that starts with a period gets a second period added (dot-stuffing). A server MUST answer an unrecognized, unimplemented or syntactically invalid command with -BAD, and a command issued in the wrong state with -ERR.
sections.plainLanguage: The client knocks on a door numbered 1038, and the two sides trade short typed lines. Every answer begins with a code that says yes, no, try later, or you said that wrong.

sections.title: Greeting and Options
sections.content:
When the connection opens, the server sends an initial status response that MUST include the response information /MTQP. A negative greeting MUST include a reason code: /unavailable or /admin. The /admin code SHOULD be used when the service is down for administrative reasons, and /unavailable for other reasons.

Any enabled options are listed as the multi-line part of the greeting, one per line. Option names are case insensitive, and names that begin with vnd. are reserved for vendor use. The only option defined here is STARTTLS, with an optional parameter required. The server MUST list it if STARTTLS is enabled and certificates are installed, and MUST give the required parameter if TLS is required for some of the domains it handles.
sections.plainLanguage: When you call, the server first says hello and lists any extra things it can do. If it is closed, it says why.

sections.title: The TRACK Command
sections.content:
The core command is TRACK unique-envid mtrk-secret. The unique-envid is defined in the companion SMTP extension, and the secret (called secret A there) is sent base64 encoded. To validate the user, the server hashes the secret with SHA1 and compares the result with the value that came with the message when it was first sent. If they match, tracking information is returned.

A successful response MUST be multi-line and consist of a MIME body part of type multipart/related whose subparts are message/tracking-status. The examples show actions such as delivered, transferred, delayed, relayed and failed, with status codes like 2.5.0 and 4.4.1.

Negative replies to TRACK can carry the reason codes /tls-required, /admin, /unavailable, /noinfo and /insecure. If the server has never seen the message, it MUST choose: either return a positive response with an action of opaque, or a negative response with /noinfo.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand over a tracking number and a secret word. If the secret matches, the server gives back a report that says whether each person's copy was delivered, passed along, delayed or failed.

sections.title: Firewalls, Timers and Pipelining
sections.content:
A firewall mail gateway has two choices for a tracking query about a host in its domain. It may reply that the message was passed on but no more is known, or it may chain the query itself, gather information from the hosts behind the firewall, and return each hop, only the final hop, or hop information with internal host names disguised. This is an administrative decision. A server that chains MUST respond within 2 minutes and SHOULD return a no-further-information answer if it cannot answer by then.

A server MAY have an inactivity autologout timer, which MUST be at least 10 minutes. A client MAY time out while waiting for a response, but its timer MUST be at least 2 minutes, since the server may be chaining queries.

Clients MAY pipeline, sending batches of commands without waiting for each reply, and the server MUST process them in order. STARTTLS must be the last command in a batch. The other commands are COMMENT, whose text is ignored and which always gets a success reply, and QUIT, which ends the session.
sections.plainLanguage: If the message went through a guarded gate, the guard can either say only that it was passed on or go ask inside for you. You can also send several questions at once, and the answers come back in order.

sections.title: TLS and Security
sections.content:
All MTQP servers MUST implement TLS, though an administrator can disable it, and it SHOULD be enabled whenever possible. The STARTTLS command takes the fully qualified domain name the client believes it is talking to, so a server hosting several domains can pick the right certificate. Possible negative codes are /unsupported, /unavailable, /tls-in-progress and /bad-fqdn. After a positive reply the client MUST start TLS negotiation before any other command.

After the handshake, the protocol resets to its initial state. Each side MUST discard knowledge gained before TLS, and the server sends a new greeting whose option list MUST NOT include STARTTLS. Both sides then decide locally whether the authentication and confidentiality achieved are good enough. A client that is unhappy SHOULD send QUIT. A server that is unhappy MAY abort, or SHOULD answer each command with -ERR and /insecure.

The Security Considerations section warns of several risks. Security depends on how random and well kept each message's secret is. Without TLS, a snoop could replay a request to learn more about a message's status. Deleting the STARTTLS option from the greeting enables a man-in-the-middle attack, which a client can detect by remembering that a server offered TLS before. Tracking is not end to end, so TLS protects only one hop. SASL is not used because authentication is per message rather than per user.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the secret word could be overheard, the two sides can agree to whisper using TLS. Anything said before whispering starts is forgotten, since someone could have tampered with it.

sections.title: The mtqp URI Scheme
sections.content:
The RFC registers a URI scheme named mtqp that performs an MTQP query and returns tracking status. It has two forms: mtqp://<mserver>/track/<unique-envid>/<mtrk-secret> for the standard port, and a form with :<port> after the server for a non-standard port. The path element /track/ is case insensitive, but the envid and secret are not. If the characters /, ? or % appear in them, they must be written as % plus two hexadecimal characters.

IANA assigned system port 1038 and registered the service name MTQP and the URI scheme. The RFC also asks IANA to keep a registry of MTQP options. Options not starting with vnd. MUST be defined in a standards track or IESG approved experimental RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The tracking number and secret can be packed into a single web-style link, so a program can open it and ask the question for you.
